title: Maybe LLM tutors might be able to work...
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou revisits four challenges she previously identified for LLM tutors (favouring questions over explanations, reducing hallucinations, beating pre-LLM technologies like textbooks, and providing classroom structure and discipline) and reports on a new Google LearnLM/Eedi study that, in her view, is 'the best answer I have seen to all four challenges.' The study, run across five UK secondary schools using the Eedi platform, compared students who got a wrong answer followed by a chat with a human tutor, a supervised LLM tutor, or a static pre-written hint, then measured success on the original question, a follow-up question, and the next unit. The LLM tutor performed roughly on par with the human tutor and clearly beat the static hint, while making errors in only 0.14% of messages. Christodoulou walks through why each of her four original challenges is addressed — the chat was structured around diagnostic questions rather than explanations, the error rate is remarkably low (though she calculates it could still mean roughly a dozen errors per student per year), and the model was embedded in a normal, teacher-led classroom rather than replacing it. She closes by connecting the study to her own company's parallel, harder struggle to get LLMs to give similarly precise, personalised feedback on student writing, where they have settled for a more limited multiple-choice 'static hint' approach in the meantime.
points: Christodoulou frames a new Google LearnLM/Eedi study as the first real answer to all four barriers she'd previously identified for LLM tutors: questions-not-explanations, hallucination rate, beating pre-LLM tech, and providing classroom structure.

The LLM tutor's measured error rate was just 0.14% (about one error per thousand messages) — comparable to what she suspects an average human teacher makes, and it clearly outperformed a static pre-written hint.

Even at 0.14%, she calculates the error rate could compound to roughly a dozen student-facing errors per year (50 messages/lesson x 5 lessons/week x 35 weeks x 0.14%), which is 'significant enough to worry about.'

She frames this study as evidence of a shift in how major tech companies approach education, contrasting it with her 2020 book's critique of Apple's and Summit Learning's evidence-free EdTech spending.

Her own company, No More Marking, is attempting a parallel but harder version of this problem for writing feedback, and has settled for a less personalised multiple-choice 'static hint' system while working toward LLM fine-tuning.
quotes: Essentially, the students got fewest questions right when taught with the 'static hint' approach. There wasn't much difference between the human tutor and the LLM tutor. The humans who supervised the LLM didn't have to make that many edits and were themselves impressed by the LLM's responses.
The most striking part of this study is that the LLM error rate was reduced down to just 0.14% - just over one error every thousand messages. This is extremely impressive.
Also, whilst one in a thousand errors sounds low, it's possible that one lesson's worth of conversation with the chatbot might include 50 or so messages, which would effectively 50x the error rate.
If we are at a point where a major technology company is committing significant resources and talent to evidence-backed principles, then there is the potential for big breakthroughs.
What should a student do if they think a chatbot has made a mistake? What process should we put in place to deal with those errors?

We are not able to get LLMs to do this reliably enough. Instead, we've settled on a different approach: the AI produces some personalised but less specific advice about the content of the writing; we create sets of multiple-choice questions about the technical aspects of writing, allocated based on scaled score; and we also have personalised AI-transcribed teacher feedback based on audio teacher comments.
